events.location: Rabat, Morocco (and UN General Assembly, New York)
events.title: Rabat summit names PLO sole Palestinian representative; Arafat addresses UN
events.summary: At the seventh Arab League summit in Rabat, Morocco (26-29 October 1974), Arab heads of state voted on 28 October to recognise the Palestine Liberation Organization as the sole legitimate representative of the Palestinian people and affirmed its right to establish a national authority on any Palestinian territory that was, in the resolution's wording, liberated. Jordan's King Hussein, whose government had claimed to speak for West Bank Palestinians, accepted the decision. On 13 November 1974 PLO chairman Yasser Arafat addressed the UN General Assembly, which had invited the PLO to its Palestine debate on 14 October, telling delegates that he came bearing an olive branch and a freedom fighter's gun. On 22 November the Assembly adopted Resolution 3236, affirming Palestinian rights to self-determination, national independence and sovereignty and the right of return, and Resolution 3237, inviting the PLO to take part in its work as an observer. Israel rejected both.

perspectives.framing: Presents Rabat and the UN appearance as international recognition of the Palestinian people as a national actor with the PLO as its sole legitimate representative, and describes the armed struggle as legitimate resistance to occupation; Arafat's speech is remembered for the 'olive branch' formula.

Rejected the PLO as a terrorist organisation committed by its covenant to Israel's destruction, opposed its admission to the General Assembly and regarded Resolution 3236 as one-sided; Israel did not recognise the PLO until 1993.
King Hussein reluctantly accepted the Rabat decision, giving up Jordan's claim to negotiate for the West Bank, while maintaining administrative and legal ties to the territory until 1988.

Describes 1974 as the year the Palestinian question returned to the General Assembly agenda as a question of the inalienable rights of a people rather than solely a refugee problem, with the PLO invited to participate as an observer.

events.title: Lebanese civil war begins with the Ain al-Rummaneh bus attack in Beirut
events.summary: On 13 April 1975 gunmen fired on a congregation outside a Maronite church in Beirut's Ain al-Rummaneh district, where Phalangist (Kataeb) leader Pierre Gemayel was attending a service, killing four people according to historians' accounts. Hours later Phalangist gunmen attacked a bus carrying Palestinians through the same district, killing 27 passengers according to most accounts, with reported figures ranging from 22 to 30. The killings ignited fighting between Christian militias and an alliance of the PLO and the leftist Lebanese National Movement, beginning a civil war that lasted until 1990. Syrian forces intervened in June 1976 and were later endorsed by the Arab League as an Arab Deterrent Force; Israel armed Christian militias and, from 1978, a client militia in the south. No central record of the dead exists: Encyclopaedia Britannica gives more than 100,000 killed, other accounts cite about 150,000, and some estimates reach 200,000 or more.

perspectives.framing: Described the fighting as a defence of Lebanese sovereignty against an armed Palestinian 'state within a state' that had drawn Israeli reprisals onto Lebanon, and portrayed the church shooting as the provocation that began the war.

Called the bus attack the 'Ain al-Rummaneh massacre' and the opening act of a Phalangist campaign against Palestinians and their Lebanese allies, framing the war as a struggle against a sectarian Maronite-dominated order.
Presented its 1976 intervention as restoring order and preventing partition of Lebanon, acting with Arab League endorsement; critics on all sides saw it as an attempt to control Lebanon and the PLO.

Generally treat the 13 April incidents as the trigger rather than the cause of a war rooted in sectarian power-sharing, socioeconomic grievances, the Palestinian armed presence after 1970 and regional rivalries.

events.title: Land Day: six Palestinian citizens of Israel killed during Galilee strike
events.summary: On 30 March 1976 Palestinian citizens of Israel held a general strike and demonstrations against a government plan to expropriate roughly 20,000 dunams (about 2,000 hectares) of land in the Galilee, much of it Arab-owned, for state and Jewish development projects. The first clashes broke out in Arraba and Deir Hanna on the evening of 29 March; on 30 March Israeli police and army units confronted protesters in Sakhnin, Arraba, Deir Hanna and other localities, and six unarmed Palestinian citizens of Israel were shot dead. Al Jazeera reports about 100 injured and hundreds arrested, while Palquest gives about 50 injured and about 300 detained. The strike was the first mass political mobilisation of Arab citizens of Israel since 1948, and the date has been commemorated annually since as Land Day (Yawm al-Ard) by Palestinians in Israel, in the occupied territories and in the diaspora. The land expropriation nonetheless proceeded.

perspectives.party: Palestinian citizens of Israel / Palestinian leadership
perspectives.framing: Commemorate Land Day as a founding moment of collective Palestinian identity inside Israel and as resistance to what they call the 'Judaization of the Galilee' and the confiscation of Arab land; the six dead are described as martyrs of the land.

Described the expropriations as lawful development of state land for the whole population, and characterised the strike as illegal disturbances incited by the Communist Party (Rakah) in which security forces responded to violent rioting.

See 1976 as the point at which Arab citizens of Israel, under military government until 1966, began organising as a national minority; the day later became a pan-Palestinian commemoration linking citizens of Israel with the occupied territories.

events.title: Likud wins Israeli election, ending Labour's dominance; Begin becomes PM
events.summary: In elections to the ninth Knesset on 17 May 1977 the right-wing Likud bloc led by Menachem Begin won 43 of 120 seats, ahead of the Labour Alignment's 32, while the new Democratic Movement for Change took 15, ending almost three decades of Labour-led government since 1948 in what Israelis called the mahapach, or upheaval. Begin, sworn in on 20 June, formed a coalition with the National Religious Party and Agudat Yisrael, appointed Labour's Moshe Dayan as foreign minister and later added the Democratic Movement for Change. The new government was ideologically committed to retaining the West Bank and expanded Israeli settlements there and in the Gaza Strip and the Golan Heights. Under Begin, Israel nonetheless entered negotiations with Egypt that produced the Camp David Accords and the 1979 peace treaty, while confrontation with the PLO in Lebanon led towards the 1982 war.

perspectives.framing: Presented the victory as a democratic revolution ending Labour's hegemony and affirming the Jewish people's right to the whole Land of Israel; Begin described Judea and Samaria as liberated, not occupied, territory.

Viewed Begin, a former Irgun commander, as an advocate of permanent Israeli control of the occupied territories, and pointed to accelerated settlement building as evidence that the autonomy offered at Camp David was not intended to lead to statehood.
The Carter administration initially feared Begin's positions would obstruct a comprehensive settlement, but later worked with him to reach the Egyptian-Israeli agreements.

events.title: Sadat visits Jerusalem and addresses the Knesset
events.summary: On 19 November 1977 Egyptian President Anwar Sadat flew to Israel, becoming the first Arab head of state to visit the country, after telling the Egyptian parliament on 9 November that he was ready to go to the ends of the earth, even to the Knesset, in search of peace. Prime Minister Menachem Begin had responded with a formal invitation. On 20 November Sadat addressed the Knesset in Jerusalem, offering peace and recognition in return for Israeli withdrawal from all territories occupied in 1967 and a solution of the Palestinian question based on self-determination; Begin replied that everything was negotiable except Jerusalem. The visit broke the Arab consensus against direct dealings with Israel: Syria, Libya, Algeria, South Yemen and the PLO condemned it and formed a Steadfastness and Confrontation Front. It opened the direct negotiations that led to the Camp David summit of September 1978.

perspectives.framing: Sadat presented the journey as a bold initiative to break the psychological barrier between Arabs and Israelis and recover Sinai, insisting he sought a comprehensive peace including Palestinian rights rather than a separate deal.

Welcomed the visit as historic recognition of Israel by the largest Arab state and as vindication of its call for direct negotiations, while rejecting full withdrawal to the 1967 lines and any Palestinian state.

Condemned the visit as a betrayal of Arab solidarity and of the Palestinian cause, and accused Sadat of pursuing a separate peace that would leave the occupation of the West Bank, Gaza and the Golan intact.
The Carter administration, which had been pursuing a Geneva conference with Soviet participation, shifted to supporting direct Egyptian-Israeli talks and later mediated them.

events.location: Southern Lebanon (Tyre-Litani area); coastal highway near Herzliya, Israel
events.title: Coastal Road attack, Operation Litani and UN Resolution 425 creating UNIFIL
events.summary: On 11 March 1978 eleven Fatah militants led by Dalal Mughrabi, landed by sea north of Tel Aviv, hijacked a bus on the coastal highway; in the fighting with Israeli forces near Herzliya 38 Israelis, including 13 children, were killed and 71 wounded, per Israeli accounts; nine attackers died. On 14 March Israel launched Operation Litani, occupying southern Lebanon up to the Litani River to push PLO fighters from the border. No authoritative Lebanese count exists: Encyclopedia.com gives about 1,500 killed and roughly 300,000 displaced in the seven-day operation, while other reference accounts cite 1,100 to 2,000 killed and 100,000 to 250,000 displaced; Israel reported about 20 soldiers killed. On 19 March the UN Security Council adopted Resolutions 425 and 426, calling for Israeli withdrawal and establishing UNIFIL, which arrived on 23 March. Israel withdrew by 13 June, handing border positions to Major Saad Haddad's militia.

perspectives.framing: Calls the bus hijacking the Coastal Road massacre, the deadliest terrorist attack in Israel to that date, and describes Operation Litani as a necessary military response to eliminate PLO bases used to attack northern Israel.

Described the seaborne raid as a commando operation against Israel led by Dalal Mughrabi, and the invasion as collective punishment of Lebanese and Palestinian civilians intended to destroy the Palestinian presence in south Lebanon.
Protested the invasion as a violation of its sovereignty causing mass displacement, and sought Security Council action to secure Israeli withdrawal and restore state authority in the south.

Resolution 425 called for strict respect for Lebanon's territorial integrity and Israel's immediate withdrawal; UNIFIL's mandate was to confirm the withdrawal, restore peace and security and help the Lebanese government regain authority, tasks it describes as obstructed by Israel's hand-over to the Haddad militia.

events.title: Camp David Accords signed by Sadat, Begin and Carter
events.summary: After thirteen days of negotiations (5-17 September 1978) hosted by US President Jimmy Carter at Camp David, Maryland, Egyptian President Anwar Sadat and Israeli Prime Minister Menachem Begin signed two framework agreements at the White House on 17 September 1978. The Framework for the Conclusion of a Peace Treaty between Egypt and Israel provided for full Israeli withdrawal from the Sinai Peninsula, demilitarised zones, free passage through the Strait of Tiran and normal relations in exchange for peace. The Framework for Peace in the Middle East proposed a five-year transitional period of full autonomy for the inhabitants of the West Bank and Gaza under an elected self-governing authority, with negotiations on final status, and invoked Security Council Resolution 242. Jordan and Palestinian representatives declined to join, and the autonomy talks later stalled. Sadat and Begin shared the 1978 Nobel Peace Prize; an Arab summit in Baghdad threatened Egypt with sanctions.

perspectives.framing: Presents the accords as a landmark of American mediation that produced the first Arab-Israeli peace and a framework, however incomplete, for resolving the Palestinian question through negotiation under Resolution 242.

Regarded the accords as securing peace with its most powerful neighbour at the price of Sinai while preserving Israeli claims in Judea and Samaria; Begin insisted that autonomy applied to inhabitants, not territory, and did not preclude settlements.

Sadat described the agreements as the path to recovering all of Sinai and as a first step toward comprehensive peace, though Egyptian foreign minister Muhammad Ibrahim Kamil resigned in protest at the weak linkage to Palestinian rights.

Rejected the accords as a separate peace concluded without Palestinian participation, and argued that 'autonomy' amounted to continued occupation; the Baghdad summit resolved to isolate Egypt if it signed a treaty.

events.title: Egypt and Israel sign peace treaty in Washington
events.summary: On 26 March 1979 Anwar Sadat and Menachem Begin signed the Egypt-Israel peace treaty at a White House ceremony before some 2,000 guests, with Jimmy Carter signing as witness, after Carter's visits to Cairo and Jerusalem earlier that month resolved a deadlock over linkage to Palestinian autonomy. The treaty, the first between Israel and an Arab state, ended the state of war existing since 1948, committed Israel to withdraw from the Sinai Peninsula in stages over three years, limited forces in defined zones, guaranteed Israeli passage through the Suez Canal and the Strait of Tiran, and provided for full diplomatic and economic relations; ambassadors were exchanged in February 1980. Most Arab states broke relations with Egypt: the Arab League suspended its membership until 1989 and moved its headquarters from Cairo to Tunis. The PLO and the Steadfastness Front denounced the treaty as a separate peace abandoning the Palestinians.

perspectives.framing: Hails the treaty as the cornerstone of Israel's security, removing the largest Arab army from the circle of war in exchange for territory, and as a model of land-for-peace with a state that recognised Israel.

Presents the treaty as the recovery of every inch of Egyptian territory through diplomacy and as fulfilment of Sadat's initiative, while stressing that Egypt continued to support Palestinian rights and the autonomy negotiations.
Condemned Egypt for breaking Arab ranks and recognising Israel without a settlement for the Palestinians, Syria or Jordan, and expelled Egypt from Arab institutions until 1989.
Regards the treaty as one of the major achievements of US diplomacy, underwritten by large annual military and economic aid to both countries and by the Multinational Force and Observers in Sinai.

events.title: Knesset passes Jerusalem Basic Law; Security Council Resolution 478 rejects it
events.summary: On 30 July 1980 the Knesset enacted the Basic Law: Jerusalem, Capital of Israel, declaring 'Jerusalem, complete and united' to be the capital of Israel and the seat of the president, Knesset, government and Supreme Court. The law consolidated the June 1967 extension of Israeli law to East Jerusalem and was passed while Egyptian-Israeli talks on Palestinian autonomy were under way, prompting Egypt to suspend them. On 20 August 1980 the UN Security Council adopted Resolution 478 by fourteen votes to none, with the United States abstaining, declaring the law null and void, affirming that it violated international law and calling on states with diplomatic missions in Jerusalem to withdraw them; the United States judged that provision non-binding. Countries with embassies in the city subsequently moved them to Tel Aviv. Israel calls Jerusalem its capital since 1949; Palestinians claim East Jerusalem as their future capital.

perspectives.framing: Describes the Basic Law as a declaratory affirmation of Jerusalem's status as the eternal, undivided capital of the Jewish people, changing nothing on the ground, and regards Resolution 478 as a political act that ignores Jewish history in the city.

Calls the law the annexation of occupied Arab Jerusalem and a violation of international law, and demands East Jerusalem, including the Haram al-Sharif / Temple Mount, as the capital of a Palestinian state.

Holds that the acquisition of territory by force is inadmissible, that East Jerusalem is occupied territory, and that measures altering the character and status of the city are null and void; Resolution 478 has been reaffirmed in later resolutions.
Protested that the law violated the spirit of the Camp David framework and suspended the autonomy negotiations in response.

events.title: Israel applies its law to the Golan Heights; Security Council Resolution 497
events.summary: On 14 December 1981 the Knesset passed the Golan Heights Law, extending Israeli law, jurisdiction and administration to the Syrian territory Israel had occupied since June 1967, in a single-day session called by Menachem Begin. The measure, widely described as annexation, replaced military government with civilian administration and offered Israeli citizenship to the plateau's Druze residents, most of whom refused it: an open general strike declared on 14 February 1982 lasted nearly six months, with residents burning Israeli identity cards, and about 80 per cent still decline citizenship. On 17 December 1981 the UN Security Council unanimously adopted Resolution 497, declaring the decision null and void, without international legal effect, and demanding its rescission. The United States suspended a recently signed strategic cooperation memorandum with Israel in protest. Syria continued to demand the return of the entire plateau to the line of 4 June 1967.

perspectives.framing: Argued that Syria had used the heights to shell Israeli communities before 1967, had rejected peace, and that applying Israeli law regularised the status of a strategically vital area; Israel avoids the word annexation and refers to the Golan as sovereign Israeli territory.
Denounces the law as illegal annexation of occupied Syrian land and insists that no peace is possible without full Israeli withdrawal from the Golan.

Resolution 497 and later General Assembly resolutions treat the Golan as occupied Syrian territory to which the Fourth Geneva Convention applies, and reject the Israeli measure as without legal effect.
Most residents declared loyalty to Syria, refused Israeli citizenship and, in 1982, held a general strike against the imposition of Israeli identity cards.

events.title: Israel completes withdrawal from Sinai under the peace treaty
events.summary: On 25 April 1982 Israel completed its withdrawal from the Sinai Peninsula, three years after signing the peace treaty, returning the final third of the territory to Egypt on schedule despite Anwar Sadat's assassination in October 1981. Earlier stages had returned El Arish in May 1979 and about two-thirds of the peninsula by January 1980. On 23 April Israeli soldiers under Defence Minister Ariel Sharon forcibly removed several hundred settlers and nationalist protesters from Yamit, the largest Sinai settlement, without casualties; Yamit and the thirteen other Sinai settlements were then largely demolished, and airfields, oil installations and Sharm el-Sheikh were handed over. President Hosni Mubarak reaffirmed the treaty, and a US-led Multinational Force and Observers began monitoring the limited-force zones. Sinai became the first territory captured in 1967 to be returned to Arab sovereignty; the Taba enclave dispute was settled by arbitration in Egypt's favour in 1988-89.

perspectives.framing: Presented the withdrawal as proof that Israel honours agreements and pays a painful territorial price for peace, while insisting that the Sinai precedent of dismantling settlements did not apply to Judea, Samaria and Gaza.
Celebrated 25 April as Sinai Liberation Day, the complete restoration of Egyptian sovereignty over its territory achieved by Sadat's initiative and confirmed under Mubarak.
Opposed the evacuation of Yamit as the uprooting of Jewish communities and a dangerous precedent; the Movement to Stop the Retreat from Sinai organised the resistance.
Noted that Egypt had regained its land while the autonomy framework for the West Bank and Gaza remained unimplemented and settlement construction accelerated.

events.title: Israel invades Lebanon (Operation Peace for Galilee) and besieges Beirut
events.summary: On 6 June 1982, after the Abu Nidal group shot its ambassador in London, Israel invaded Lebanon in an operation it named Peace for Galilee, stating the aim of pushing PLO forces 40 kilometres from the border. More than 40,000 troops entered by land, sea and air, advanced far beyond that line, fought Syrian units in the Beqaa Valley and by 13 June encircled West Beirut, the PLO's base. The siege, with water and electricity cut off, lasted until a ceasefire on 12 August. Security Council Resolution 509 of 6 June demanded withdrawal. Lebanese police figures cited by news agencies put deaths in Lebanon by late August at about 17,800; an estimate cited by RTE gives about 19,000 killed, 5,500 of them West Beirut civilians; Israel disputed such figures. The IDF reported 368 soldiers killed by the end of the siege, and 1,216 between June 1982 and May 1985.

perspectives.framing: Presented Operation Peace for Galilee as a defensive war to end PLO rocket and terrorist attacks on northern Israel after the July 1981 ceasefire, later expanded by Defence Minister Ariel Sharon to remove the PLO and Syrian forces from Lebanon; Israeli critics called it a war of choice.

Describes the invasion as an attempt to destroy the Palestinian national movement and the refugee camps, and the ten-week defence of Beirut as heroic resistance that ended only when Lebanese allies asked the PLO to leave.

Successive Lebanese governments condemned the invasion and occupation, while Phalangist leaders under Bashir Gemayel welcomed the removal of the PLO and were elected to the presidency in August 1982 with Israeli support.

Resolution 509 demanded that Israel withdraw immediately and unconditionally to Lebanon's internationally recognised boundaries; UNIFIL positions were overrun and the force's mandate could not be carried out.

events.title: PLO fighters and leadership evacuated from Beirut; Arafat departs for Tunis
events.summary: Under a plan negotiated by US envoy Philip Habib and agreed on 18 August 1982, Palestinian fighters began leaving West Beirut on 21 August, when several hundred sailed for Cyprus under a US, French and Italian multinational force. Yasser Arafat sailed on 30 August aboard a Greek cruise ship bound for Athens and then Tunis, and the evacuation ended on 1 September, ahead of schedule. Contemporary US and press accounts put the number of PLO and Palestine Liberation Army fighters evacuated at roughly 8,000 to 11,000, with about 3,600 Syrian soldiers, dispersed to Syria, Tunisia, Jordan, Iraq, Sudan, the two Yemens and Algeria; Al Majalla, citing released documents, gives about 8,500 PLO members sent to Tunisia and 7,587 to Syria. The PLO's headquarters moved to Tunis. The United States gave written assurances that civilians left in the camps would be protected; the multinational force departed by 10 September.

perspectives.framing: Presented the departure as an honourable withdrawal after a two-month defence of Beirut, undertaken to spare the city, and accused the United States and Israel of breaking guarantees for the safety of the civilians left behind.

Described the evacuation as the achievement of the war's central aim, the expulsion of the PLO's military infrastructure from Lebanon, and later argued that the PLO's dispersal to Tunis weakened it politically.

Credited the Habib mission with ending the siege without a battle for the city, and framed the multinational force as a short-term guarantor of a peaceful evacuation rather than a peacekeeping presence.

The Lebanese government and most Lebanese factions sought the PLO's departure to end the siege and restore state authority, while Palestinian residents of the camps feared retaliation once the fighters left.

events.location: Sabra and Shatila, West Beirut, Lebanon
events.title: Sabra and Shatila massacre in Israeli-controlled West Beirut
events.summary: From the evening of 16 September to the afternoon of 18 September 1982, two days after President-elect Bashir Gemayel's assassination, Lebanese Phalangist (Kataeb) militiamen entered the Sabra neighbourhood and the adjoining Shatila Palestinian refugee camp in West Beirut and killed Palestinian and Lebanese civilians over roughly 43 hours. Israeli forces, in West Beirut since 15 September, surrounded the camps, admitted the militia and fired illumination flares at night. Israel's Kahan Commission estimated 700 to 800 dead; the Palestinian Red Crescent reported more than 2,000; historian Bayan Nuwayhed al-Hout documented at least 1,300 named victims and estimated a maximum of 3,500. The UN Security Council condemned the killings in Resolution 521 on 19 September, and the General Assembly in December termed them an act of genocide. In February 1983 the Kahan Commission found Israel indirectly responsible and Ariel Sharon personally responsible, leading to his resignation; no Phalangist was prosecuted.

perspectives.framing: Describes the killings as a massacre of defenceless refugees carried out under Israeli protection after the fighters had left on US guarantees, and holds Israel and its commanders directly responsible alongside the Phalange.

Accepted the Kahan Commission's finding of indirect responsibility for failing to foresee and stop the militia, while stressing that the killings were committed by Lebanese Phalangists and denying that Israeli soldiers took part; some Israelis at the time called the inquiry a model of accountability.
Denied ordering a massacre, portraying the entry into the camps as a search for remaining fighters after Gemayel's assassination; the party has never accepted institutional responsibility.

Resolution 521 condemned 'the criminal massacre of Palestinian civilians in Beirut'; General Assembly resolution 37/123 D of 16 December 1982 resolved that the massacre was an act of genocide, a characterisation contested by Israel and several Western states.

events.title: Beirut bombings of 1983 and the emergence of Hezbollah
events.summary: On 23 October 1983 two truck bombs struck the barracks of the US Marine contingent at Beirut airport and a French paratroop base, killing 241 US service members and 58 French soldiers, according to their governments, along with several Lebanese civilians, the Marine Corps' largest single-day loss since Iwo Jima. On 18 April 1983 a car bomb had destroyed the US embassy in Beirut, killing 63 people. A group calling itself Islamic Jihad claimed the attacks; the United States attributed them to Lebanese Shia militants organised with Iranian Revolutionary Guard support, the network that became Hezbollah, which emerged after the 1982 Israeli invasion and published its founding open letter in February 1985. Hezbollah denies responsibility for the 1983 bombings. The multinational force withdrew in February 1984, the Israel-Lebanon agreement of 17 May 1983 collapsed, and Hezbollah's armed campaign against Israeli forces in southern Lebanon began.

perspectives.framing: Describes the barracks bombing as the deadliest terrorist attack on Americans before 2001, attributes it to Hezbollah acting with Iranian direction, and designated Hezbollah a foreign terrorist organisation in 1997.

Presents itself as an Islamic resistance movement born of the 1982 invasion to expel Israeli and Western forces from Lebanon, denies involvement in the 1983 bombings, and describes attacks on foreign troops in Lebanon as resistance to occupation.
Regards Hezbollah as an Iranian proxy created to wage war on Israel from Lebanon, and cites its attacks on Israeli forces from 1983 onward as justification for maintaining the security zone.
Acknowledges supporting the formation of Hezbollah as part of Islamic resistance to Israel and Western intervention, while denying operational responsibility for the Beirut bombings.

events.title: Israel withdraws to a self-declared 'security zone' in southern Lebanon
events.summary: Following a cabinet decision announced by Defence Minister Yitzhak Rabin on 14 January 1985, Israel withdrew most of its forces from Lebanon, leaving Sidon in February, the Beqaa and Nabatiyeh areas in April, and completing the pullback in June, dated 10 June in most accounts. It retained a strip along the border averaging about 10 kilometres wide, up to 20 kilometres in places, which it called the security zone, policed by an IDF garrison with the South Lebanon Army militia, an outgrowth of Saad Haddad's forces, under General Antoine Lahad. The withdrawal, prompted by mounting casualties and domestic opposition, followed the collapse of the 17 May 1983 agreement and a growing guerrilla campaign by Shia militias including Hezbollah. Israel said the zone protected its northern towns; Lebanon and the United Nations regarded it as continued occupation contrary to Resolution 425. Fighting continued there until Israel's full withdrawal in May 2000.

perspectives.framing: Presented the security zone as a limited defensive buffer to keep attackers away from Israel's northern border after the failure of the 1983 agreement, and the SLA as a local Lebanese partner.
Called the zone an occupation to be ended by resistance, and treated the 1985 withdrawal as the first fruit of its armed campaign; the SLA was described as a collaborationist militia.
The Lebanese government demanded complete Israeli withdrawal under Resolution 425 and did not recognise the SLA, while residents of the zone lived under a mixed Israeli-SLA administration.
UNIFIL reported that Israel's continued control of the zone prevented it from fulfilling its mandate, and the Security Council repeatedly reiterated its call for full withdrawal.

boundaryChanges.description: Syrian forces enter Lebanon in strength; by the Riyadh and Cairo summits of October 1976 a mainly Syrian Arab Deterrent Force controls most of Lebanon outside the Christian-held areas of East Beirut and Mount Lebanon and the south, where Israel backs local militias.
Operation Litani: Israeli forces occupy southern Lebanon up to the Litani River (excluding the Tyre pocket) from 14-21 March 1978.

Israel completes its withdrawal from Lebanon under Resolution 425 but hands a border strip to the militia of Major Saad Haddad (later the South Lebanon Army); UNIFIL deploys in the area between the Litani and the Haddad enclave.

Israel begins the staged withdrawal from Sinai required by the peace treaty, returning El Arish and the northern coastal strip to Egypt; interim lines move west-to-east across the peninsula over the following months.
Israel completes the interim withdrawal to the El Arish-Ras Muhammad line, returning about two-thirds of the Sinai Peninsula to Egyptian control; ambassadors are exchanged the following month.

Basic Law: Jerusalem, Capital of Israel declares united Jerusalem the capital; no change in control on the ground (East Jerusalem has been under Israeli law since June 1967) but a formalisation rejected by Security Council Resolution 478.

Golan Heights Law extends Israeli law, jurisdiction and administration to the occupied Golan Heights (annexation in effect); Security Council Resolution 497 declares the measure null and void. Mapped as israeli-annexed from this date.

Israel completes withdrawal from the Sinai Peninsula; Egypt resumes sovereignty over all of Sinai except the disputed Taba enclave (returned after arbitration in March 1989). The Multinational Force and Observers monitors limited-force zones.
Israeli forces occupy southern Lebanon up to the outskirts of Beirut and the Beirut-Damascus highway, push Syrian forces back in the Beqaa, and encircle West Beirut (siege 13 June-21 August 1982).

Israeli forces withdraw from West Beirut after the Sabra and Shatila massacre; the US-French-Italian multinational force redeploys to Beirut, while Israel continues to hold the south up to the Chouf and Beirut-Damascus road.
Israel withdraws from the Chouf mountains to a line along the Awali River north of Sidon; fighting between Druze and Christian militias follows in the Chouf.

Israel completes a three-stage withdrawal (Sidon, February; Beqaa and Nabatiyeh, April; final stage 10 June 1985) to a self-declared security zone about 10-20 km deep along the border, held jointly with the South Lebanon Army until May 2000.

uncertainties: VERIFICATION PASS 2026-09-14: WebSearch corroboration only (pages cannot be fetched in this sandbox). Every source URL now cited appeared in a WebSearch result run during this pass; all previously cited URLs (Britannica topic pages, undocs.org, unispal history pages, UNIFIL background, Knesset, Avalon, Times of Israel topic page, cfr.org singular path) were replaced because they did not surface in results. The session's search budget was exhausted after 22 searches, before the Lebanese-casualty, Sinai-completion-date, PLO-evacuation-count and 1985-withdrawal-date follow-up searches could run; the six events left verified:false are listed below and should be re-checked when budget is available.

1975-04-13-lebanese-civil-war-begins: date and place corroborated (France 24, Al Majalla, Gulf Today, MERIP, Britannica), but the bus-attack toll of 27 appeared in only one search-result text, the church-shooting toll of 4 was not corroborated, and total war-death estimates diverge (Britannica >100,000; others 150,000; up to 200,000; one account 150,000-250,000).

1978-03-11-coastal-road-attack-operation-litani-unifil: the 38 Israeli dead (13 children), 71 wounded and 9 of 11 attackers killed are corroborated (Times of Israel, HRW, IDF). Lebanese/Palestinian deaths in Operation Litani are corroborated only by Encyclopedia.com (about 1,500 killed, about 300,000 displaced); the 1,100-2,000 / 100,000-250,000 range and the roughly 20 Israeli military deaths appeared only in non-citable mirror sites.

1982-04-25-israel-completes-sinai-withdrawal: the Yamit evacuation of 23 April 1982 is corroborated (Washington Post, JVL, Washington Institute, CSMonitor), and a CSMonitor report dated 26 April 1982 is consistent with completion on 25 April, but no search-result text explicitly stated the 25 April date, the Sharm el-Sheikh handover, the MFO deployment or the Taba arbitration.

1982-06-06-israel-invades-lebanon: date, forces (over 40,000 troops) and the two-month siege are corroborated (IDF, RTE, JVL, ADL). The Lebanese police figure of about 17,825 killed and the IDF figure of 368 soldiers killed by the end of the siege were not found in this pass; results gave an estimate of about 19,000 killed including 5,500 civilians in West Beirut (cited by RTE) and 1,216 Israeli soldiers killed 5 June 1982-31 May 1985. Resolution 509 was not corroborated.

1982-08-21-plo-evacuation-from-beirut: dates (agreement 18 August, first departures 21 August, Arafat 30 August, completion 1 September) are corroborated (CSMonitor, JTA, i24NEWS, Al Majalla, Facts on File). Evacuee counts conflict: the 8,000-11,000 fighters and 3,600 Syrians in the file were not corroborated, while Al Majalla gives about 8,500 PLO members to Tunisia and 7,587 to Syria, at odds with other accounts that place most evacuees in Syria.

1985-06-10-israel-withdraws-to-south-lebanon-security-zone: the 14 January 1985 cabinet decision, January-June withdrawal, security zone (averaging about 10 km wide) and SLA role are corroborated (CRS, Times of Israel, ECF), but the three-stage sequence and the 10 June (or 6 June) completion date were not stated in search-result content.

1974-10-28: the Rabat summit met 26-29 October 1974; the vote is dated 28 October in most accounts, while Palquest dates the Palestine Resolution text 29 October. The voting record on Resolutions 3236 and 3237 (Israel and the United States against) was not restated in results and has been removed from the summary.
1976-03-30 Land Day: injured reported as about 100 (Al Jazeera) or about 50 (Palquest); arrests as 'hundreds' or about 300. Both are shown side by side.

1980-07-30 Jerusalem Basic Law: one result (UNSCR.com) refers to the Knesset's 29 July enactment while ECF and others give 30 July; 30 July is used. The number of embassies that left Jerusalem (usually given as 13) was not corroborated and has been removed from the summary.

1981-12-14 Golan Heights Law: one result dates the Knesset vote (63-21) to 15 December 1981; 14 December is used. The Druze population figure (about 13,000; estimates 12,000-15,000) and the US suspension of the strategic cooperation memorandum were not corroborated in this pass; the population figure has been removed from the summary.

1982-09-16 Sabra and Shatila: death-toll estimates diverge sharply - 700-800 (Kahan Commission), more than 2,000 (Palestinian Red Crescent), at least 1,300 named victims and up to 3,500 (Bayan Nuwayhed al-Hout). The Lebanese authorities' count of about 460 bodies was not corroborated and was moved to a note. Killing ran from about 6 pm on 16 September to about 1 pm on 18 September (43 hours).

1983-10-23 Beirut bombings: 241 US and 58 French dead corroborated (Britannica, CNN, State Department, The National); the breakdown 220 Marines / 18 sailors / 3 soldiers and the 17 Americans among the 63 embassy dead were not restated in results; the latter has been removed from the summary.
1977-11-19 Sadat visit: Sadat landed in Israel on the evening of 19 November 1977 and addressed the Knesset on 20 November; the event is dated to the arrival.

1979-03-26 peace treaty: the exact date of the Arab League suspension (27 March 1979) was not restated in results; the summary now says only that Egypt was suspended until 1989 and the headquarters moved to Tunis.
